checkpoints: State shape: `presence:(room, user)` maps to a SET of connection ids; online means the set is non-empty.
Justification: a boolean can't distinguish "closed one of two tabs" from "fully offline", and a bare counter can't dedupe a connection id being re-added.

Contract: `add(connId)` returns `firstConnection` (true when the set moves empty->non-empty); `remove(connId)` returns `lastConnection` (true when the set moves non-empty->empty, and the key gets deleted); `listOnline(room)` returns the current online list.

Callers: the join handler calls `add`; server-side disconnect handling calls `remove`; the join ack carries `listOnline`'s result directly so the joining client renders immediately without waiting on a broadcast round-trip back to itself.
Eventing rule: broadcast `user-joined` only when `firstConnection` is true, and `user-left` only when `lastConnection` is true -- every other tab open/close stays silent, guarding against flicker.
Failure story: if the server process crashes before the disconnect handler runs, a connection id stays stuck in the set forever, producing ghost presence.
Mitigation for the crash: a TTL on every presence key plus periodic heartbeat renewal expires ghost entries even when no disconnect event ever fires.
Scaling requirement: in a multi-node deployment the set must live on a shared store (e.g. Redis) so the contract holds across every instance.

Identity: the server stamps every message with a per-room monotonic seq at the moment it's appended to the log, atomically allocated via an in-process counter (single writer), a DB sequence (BIGSERIAL), or an atomic Redis INCR (multiple writers)

The ordering key must never be the client's own number or a wall-clock timestamp, since clock drift and genuinely concurrent sends mean only a single atomically-incrementing server-side authority can guarantee one total order

Cursor: the client owns lastSeq, its private record of how far it has seen, persisting it per room (e.g. a localStorage key keyed by room ID) so a refresh or restart doesn't reset it to zero, and resends that same lastSeq the moment it reconnects; the server keeps no memory of any individual client's position
Events, write path: join(room,user) -> ack confirms entry; chat(text) -> the server assigns the next seq and broadcasts message{seq,sender,text,ts} to everyone in the room
Events, resume path: replay-since(room,lastSeq) -> ack{messages[]} is a request/response over the same socket addressed back to the one reconnecting client, not a room-wide broadcast
Semantics: the filter is strictly seq > lastSeq, never >=, so the client's own last-seen message is never resent as a duplicate

The guarantee is at-least-once, not exactly-once, because a flaky network can cause the same replay to be requested twice; the client's merge logic must dedupe by the pair (room, seq) and only ever advance lastSeq forward, never letting it regress on a stale or out-of-order ack

Bounds: the replay ack is capped to a fixed batch so a long-offline client doesn't trigger one enormous reply; anything beyond the cap is a separate, paginated fetch by cursor against durable storage, not this contract's job
These are two independent bugs, not one single fix that covers both
Cross-room leak root cause: the handler emits at server-wide scope, calling emit with no room key attached, so the event reaches every connected socket regardless of room
Cross-room leak fix: scope the emit to the correct room label, since the room is the fanout partition key that decides who receives the event, not who happens to be online

Stale-room delivery is a separate root cause: the joinRoom handler only joins the new room without leaving the previous one first, so the socket legitimately remains a member of both rooms at once and receives the old room's broadcast by the rules, not due to an emit-layer bug
Stale-room fix: leave the previous room before joining the new one, preserving the one-room-per-socket model

The scope ladder for emits has three rungs — server-wide (every connected socket), room-wide including the sender, and room-wide excluding the sender — and picking the wrong rung is exactly how both cross-room leaks and self-echo bugs happen in practice
Verification: stand up two independent clients in two different rooms, send a message from one, and assert it appears only in that room and never in the other

The auth middleware verifies the JWT exactly once at the handshake, so the 15-minute exp silently passes during a chat session that routinely lasts hours, since nothing actively re-checks it afterward

Proactive pattern: the server computes time remaining to exp from the already-verified payload, sets a timer, and near expiry emits an event like auth-refresh-required; the client calls the REST refresh endpoint for a fresh token and reconnects, with essentially no visible interruption

Reactive pattern: the server force-closes the connection once exp has passed; the client listens for the disconnect and reconnects with a fresh token — simpler to build, at the cost of a small, visible blip
Choosing between the two patterns is a trade-off between smooth UX and implementation complexity
Skipping exp tracking altogether is a security hole: it would let a stolen or already-revoked (logged-out) token keep an authenticated connection alive on an open socket almost indefinitely
A short exp (e.g. 15 minutes) bounds that blast radius, and every re-auth/reconnect is a natural checkpoint to verify the token hasn't been revoked
Checking the token in every handler is not the same security with less machinery — it is weaker security with more recurring cost

Cost axis: the handshake fires exactly once per connection so the cryptographic verify happens once no matter how long the socket lives, whereas per-handler checking pays one signature check per event, scaling with chat throughput and getting worse the busier the room

Safety axis: per-handler checking still lets the connection get accepted before any check runs, leaving a window where an unauthenticated socket sits in the server's connection set able to receive lifecycle notifications and broadcasts; handshake-level rejection removes that window because the socket is never added to the connection set in the first place

Semantics axis: rejecting at the handshake gives a clean connection-level error and the socket never becomes connected, so nothing downstream has to unwind bad state; rejecting inside a handler means the connection already went through its accept lifecycle, so the server must manually tear the socket down after the connect event already fired for an unauthenticated identity

On success, the payload is attached to the connection's per-socket state a single time, and every handler for the rest of that connection's life reads the identity back from there instead of re-verifying

This is not specific to one library: whatever the stack calls it — handshake middleware, an interceptor on the CONNECT frame, bearer authorization at connection negotiation, or verifying before the protocol upgrade completes — the shape is always reject-before-accept, because a durable connection gets only one natural moment to authenticate cheaply

Auto-reconnect lives entirely at the transport layer, redialing the channel with backoff and jitter, but replays no messages at all because the server has no way of knowing which message the client last saw unless the client tells it
That is exactly the boundary between reconnectable and lossless: a live channel does not mean data lost while offline magically comes back
Minimal mechanism, server side: the server numbers every message with a monotonically increasing per-room seq and keeps them in a log
Minimal mechanism, client side: the client persists lastSeq, the cursor marking the last message it saw, and proactively resends exactly that number the moment the channel comes back up
Minimal mechanism, resume: the server filters the log for every message with seq strictly greater than lastSeq and acks the whole batch back

The guarantee achieved is at-least-once: a flaky network can drive more than one disconnect/reconnect cycle, so the same replay batch can be delivered more than once, so the client must dedupe by the key pair (room, seq) and only ever move lastSeq forward, never regressing even on a duplicate delivery

Exactly-once requires one step further: a clientMsgId generated by the client and attached to every outgoing message, plus an idempotent insert-if-not-already-present on the server keyed by that id, so the same message is recorded exactly once no matter how many times it is resent

For a chat app that only needs to display the right content, client-side dedupe by (room, seq) already neutralizes duplicates; exactly-once is only worth its extra cost when a duplicate causes an irreversible side effect on the server, like charging money twice or sending the same email twice

Root cause: room membership lives only in EACH process's own in-memory state — server.to(room).emit() on node A can only enumerate sockets currently connected to node A itself, with no visibility into other nodes

Why intermittent: the load balancer assigns connections with no room-awareness, so two people in the same room land on the same node (looks fine) or different nodes (broadcast can't cross the process boundary) purely by chance

The fix: an adapter bridges nodes over a shared pub/sub bus (commonly Redis) — every emit is published onto the bus, and every other node subscribes and re-emits it to its own local sockets in that room
Sticky sessions at the load balancer pin a connection's handshake and lifecycle to one node, which is a related but distinct technique from the pub/sub adapter
Cost side A: the adapter adds operational overhead — a new piece of infrastructure to run plus one extra pub/sub hop of latency on every broadcast
Cost side B: the bus becomes a new single point of failure — if it goes down, cross-node fanout breaks even though each node is individually healthy

Senior judgment is quantified, not absolute: a single strong-enough node can hold tens of thousands of idle connections, so vertical scaling stays the cheaper/simpler choice until connection count or real HA needs exceed that
The same per-node trap generalizes: presence and typing-indicator state are exactly as node-local as room membership, so moving to multi-node must move that state to a shared store too

In this handler, the sender's own userId round-trips back because the relay broadcasts to the whole room via `this.server.to(roomId)`, which addresses every socket connected to the gateway that has joined that room — including the socket that just sent the event.

The client-side rendering logic is not at fault: it correctly displays whatever userId arrives in the payload, self included, so the defect lives entirely in the server's broadcast scope on the relay line, not in how the UI interprets the event.

Two broadcast scopes exist for any room in Socket.IO: `server.to(room)` (or `io.to(room)`), which reaches every socket in the room including the emitter, and `client.to(room)` (called on the sender's own connected socket), which reaches every other socket in the room but excludes the emitter itself.

The one-line fix is replacing `this.server.to(body.roomId).emit(...)` with `client.to(body.roomId).emit(...)` — swapping the server-wide handle for the connected socket's own `.to()` call switches the scope from room-inclusive to room-except-sender.

Typing indicators are a signal meant for other participants only: the person typing already has local UI state confirming they are typing, so echoing the event back to them serves no purpose and produces the reported bug.

This differs from a presence/join broadcast, where using the room-inclusive scope (`server.to(room)`) is correct because a newly joined user should also see themselves reflected as online immediately — the correct scope depends on whether the event is meant to include or exclude its own sender.

The typing feature stays ephemeral regardless of which scope is used — no state is persisted to a store, and the receiving client's UI clears the indicator itself after a short debounce window with no new event, so the fix does not require adding any cleanup logic.

A correct regression test needs two connected clients in the same room: after the sender emits typing, the test must assert both that the other client's indicator shows the sender's name and that the sender's own indicator stays empty — checking only the receiver's side would pass even with the buggy inclusive-scope code.
On the server, `replaySince` filters with `m.seq >= lastSeq`, an inclusive boundary that re-includes the exact message the client already holds instead of starting the replay after it.
Since `lastSeq` represents "the last message the client already has," the replay comparison must be strictly greater-than (`m.seq > lastSeq`) so the boundary message is never resent.

Tracing concrete numbers shows the mechanism: a client at `lastSeq = 4` reconnects and emits `replay-since` with `lastSeq: 4`; the inclusive filter returns `[4, 5, 6]`, so message 4 reappears even though it was already displayed.

The client's reconnect handler appends `ack.messages` straight onto the existing list with `[...prev, ...ack.messages]` and has no dedupe keyed by `(roomId, seq)`, so any resent boundary message gets rendered again.

Because `lastSeq` is re-derived from the last item of each ack (`ack.messages.at(-1)?.seq`), the same off-by-one boundary reproduces on every reconnect — two blips therefore compound into two duplicate copies rather than one static duplicate.

Fixing only the server's comparison operator is not enough: at-least-once delivery over a flaky connection can legitimately trigger `replay-since` more than once for the same gap (for example, a disconnect right after the ack but before the client persists the new `lastSeq`), so the client must independently guard against duplicates.

Client-side defense requires tracking already-rendered messages by a composite key such as `${roomId}:${seq}`, skipping any incoming message whose key is already present, and advancing `lastSeq` only forward (e.g. `Math.max(lastSeq, incoming.seq)`) rather than trusting whatever the latest ack reports.

The fix should be proven with two regression tests: a single disconnect/reconnect asserting the message count stays exactly N with no extra copy, and a double reconnect with no new messages sent in between asserting the list is byte-for-byte unchanged — showing the merge itself is idempotent, not just the boundary condition.

Once a handshake middleware verifies a JWT and attaches the resulting identity to the connection (for example `client.data.user` in Socket.IO), every later handler on that connection must read identity from that server-set state, not from fields inside the client-supplied message body.

Re-reading an identity field such as `username` out of the message body reopens a trust boundary that authentication already closed, letting any connected client claim to be another user in a broadcast.

A crafted body such as `{ username: 'alice', room: 'admin-only', text: '...' }` sent through an ordinary client tool (browser DevTools or a raw socket emit) gets broadcast by the server exactly as submitted whenever the handler emits `body.username` and `body.room` without cross-checking them.

Joining a room and broadcasting into a room are two separate operations; recording `client.data.room` inside a `joinRoom` handler has no protective effect on a separate `chatToServer` handler unless that handler explicitly reads the stored value back and compares it against the room in the incoming message.

Without a check tying the emit's target room to the room the connection actually joined, a socket can broadcast into rooms it was never authorized to enter, since `client.join()` at connect time and `server.to(body.room).emit()` at message time are wired to different, unrelated sources of truth for "room".

Replacing `body.username` with `client.data.user.username` in the emit removes the identity-forgery path entirely, because the broadcast then always carries the JWT-derived name no matter what value the client places in the message body.

Rejecting messages where `body.room` does not match the connection's recorded `client.data.room` closes the room-injection path; an equally valid and simpler version of the same fix is to ignore the body's room field entirely and always broadcast to the stored `client.data.room`.

Proving the fix requires an adversarial test rather than a happy-path one: connect as one user who never joins the target room, emit a message claiming a different username and that room, then assert the resulting broadcast carries the real JWT-derived username and either never reaches the unauthorized room or is rejected outright.
